The sound & smell check: squirrel, raccoon, or skunk?

You don't need to go up and look — in fact, please don't. Just tell us what you've been hearing, smelling, and seeing. Three quick picks, and we'll tell you which guest you've most likely got. Skunks rarely climb into attics — their giveaway is a den under a deck, porch, or shed, and that unmistakable smell. It's a good first guess, not a diagnosis; the inspection confirms it.

Meet the usual suspects

Almost every call in the GTA turns out to be one of these three. Two of them move into the attic; the third dens underneath the house instead. They sound — and smell — different, and they're handled a little differently, which is why each gets its own page.

the daytime guest

Squirrels

Busy at sunrise and again before dinner, quiet overnight. If your attic sounds like a tiny construction crew that clocks off at dusk, it's probably squirrels.

  • Scratching and scampering overhead during the day
  • Chewed vents, soffits, and wiring — the wiring is the worrying part
  • In spring, a nest of pups that can't leave on their own yet
the nighttime guest

Raccoons

Toronto's most famous attic tenant. Heavy, slow, and surprisingly strong — if it sounds like a person up there at 2 a.m., and shingles or soffits look torn, think raccoon.

  • Thumping and walking sounds after dark
  • Torn shingles, bent vents, a damaged chimney cap
  • In spring, a mother with kits — she will not leave without them
the under-deck guest

Skunks

Not an attic animal — a skunk wants a quiet, dark den at ground level: under a deck, porch, shed, or concrete steps. You usually smell this guest long before you ever see it.

  • A strong, musky skunk smell around the deck or yard, worst at night
  • A den opening dug under a deck, porch, shed, or steps
  • Small cone-shaped holes dug in the lawn overnight, hunting grubs
  • In late spring, kits following their mother in a line at dusk

Tonight, before anyone comes out

You found this page at an annoying hour, most likely. Here's the short version of what helps and what makes it worse — the full fix can wait for daylight and a ladder that isn't yours.

Do this

  • Note the times and sounds. “Loud at 6 a.m., quiet at night” is genuinely useful — it's how the pro tells squirrel from raccoon before arriving.
  • Look from the ground. A chewed vent or lifted soffit spotted from the driveway is worth mentioning in your request.
  • Keep pets and kids away from the attic hatch and any droppings you find.
  • Send the request when you're ready. The details you share now make the callback short.
  • Bring dogs in at dusk, and check the yard first. Skunks are out after dark, they're slow and nearly blind up close — and a surprised skunk sprays. A quick look with a light on saves everyone the bath.

Please don't

  • Don't go into the attic to check. A cornered mother raccoon is not a fair fight, and raccoon droppings can carry roundworm.
  • Don't block the hole yourself. Seal an animal — or its babies — inside and a small problem becomes a much bigger, sadder one.
  • Don't use poison or mothballs. They don't work on attic wildlife, they're a hazard in your home, and an animal dying in a wall cavity is nobody's solution.
  • Don't just wait for spring. Dens with young can last months, and the chewing and damage build the whole time.
  • Don't corner a skunk, and don't block the gap under your deck. Cornering is what triggers a spray, and sealing a den shut can trap kits inside — a smell problem no one wants, right under the porch.

How getting help works

From your side of the ceiling, it's three steps — and none of them involve you on a roof.

step one

Tell us what's happening

Two minutes on one short form: which animal (or “not sure”), where you're hearing it, how urgent it feels, and whether babies might be up there. That's the information a pro actually needs.

step two

A short callback & a look

A local wildlife pro calls back to confirm the details, then inspects the attic and roofline — every entry point, and whether there are young. You get a firm price after that inspection, not a guess over the phone.

step three

Out, sealed, done

A one-way door lets the animals leave on their own; babies are reunited with their mother outside; then every entry is sealed with chew-proof materials so next season doesn't start the same way.

What affects the price

There is no firm price on this page — on purpose. Every attic is different, so the price is set by the pro who inspects your home, after they have seen the entries, the access, and whether there are young. What we can show you honestly is what that price is based on: the factors below.

Why no number before an inspection: the simplest job — one animal, one easy entry, no babies, no cleanup — is a very different job from a den with young, several entry points, and damage to repair. Guessing a number before anyone has looked would not be fair to you or to the pro who has to honour it. That is why the firm price is confirmed after inspection only.

What changes the price

These are the factors that most often affect the total. Your pro prices your actual entries, access, babies, and damage after looking.

1 · Number of entry points

One chewed vent is a smaller job than several gaps at the roofline, soffits, and chimney. Every entry needs to be found and sealed in chew-proof material, so more entries means more time, materials, and cost.

2 · Attic access & roof height

A low, easy-to-reach roof with clear attic access is quicker and safer to work on. Steep, high, or awkward roofs, and tight or obstructed attics, take longer and can require extra equipment.

3 · Babies in the attic

In baby season, young can’t use a one-way door. They need to be carefully placed outside by the entry so their mother can reunite with and relocate them, with extra checks — which adds time and visits.

4 · Size & severity of the problem

A single animal that arrived last week is different from an established den, several animals, or damage built up over months. Property size, how far the animals have spread, and how long they’ve been there all affect the work needed.

5 · Sealing, cleanup & insulation

Removal is only part of the job. Sealing and prevention work, removing droppings and soiled nesting, decontamination, and replacing contaminated insulation are usually priced separately — and a badly soiled attic can cost more to put right than the removal itself.

6 · Damage that needs repair

Torn soffits and fascia, chewed vents or wiring, and a damaged or missing chimney cap are repairs on top of removal. The extent of that damage is itemised on the quote after inspection.

Two things to confirm when you get a quote

Emergency / after-hours fees: don’t assume there is a surcharge — or that there isn’t one. Ask when you call.

Tax: confirm whether tax is included in your written quote.

Removed kindly, or not at all.

This is the part we won't compromise on, and Ontario law backs it up. A trapped wild animal in Ontario has to be released within 1 km of where it was caught, within 24 hours — which means trap-and-dump doesn't even work: the animal comes straight back, stressed, to a home it knows.

So the method here is different: one-way doors and sealing. The animals walk out on their own, find the door won't let them back in, and move on to one of the backup dens they already have. In baby season, the young are placed safely by the entry in a warm reunion box, and mother moves them herself — usually the same night. Nobody gets hurt. Nobody gets orphaned. You get your attic back.

Questions everyone asks first

Can't I just wait for them to leave on their own?

Sometimes a lone animal moves on — but a den with young can stay occupied for months, and autumn brings a second wave looking for winter shelter. Meanwhile squirrels keep chewing (wiring included) and raccoon damage and droppings keep building. Waiting is a gamble, not a plan.

Is it ever okay to seal the hole myself?

Only if you are completely sure nothing is inside — and in baby season, you almost never can be. Sealing a mother out while her young are inside, or sealing animals in, creates a far worse problem than the one you started with. This is exactly the part worth handing to a pro.

Will they come back next year?

The animals will try — your attic was warm and safe, and they remember it. That's why the job isn't finished at removal: every entry point gets sealed and weak spots (vents, soffits, chimney) get screened or capped. Sealing is what makes it a one-time fix instead of an annual subscription.

What if I'm renting?

Tell us in the form — there's an option for tenants and landlords. Wildlife in the structure is generally the property owner's responsibility, and a clear written request (which is what the form prepares) is a useful thing to pass to your landlord.

There's a strong smell but no attic noise — could that be a skunk?

Very likely, yes. Skunks den at ground level — under decks, porches, sheds, and steps — rather than in attics, so the signs are a musky smell that's strongest at night, a dug opening under a structure, and small holes dug in the lawn. Don't block the opening yourself: kits may be inside, and a cornered skunk sprays. The skunk page explains how a one-way door on the den and digging-proof screening end it.

How much will mine actually cost?

That is confirmed after inspection — there is no fixed price listed here. Where yours lands depends mainly on how many entry points need sealing, attic access and roof height, whether there are babies, how established the problem is, and whether sealing, cleanup, insulation, or repairs are needed on top. That is why the firm price comes after the inspection, not before — and why tax should be confirmed in the written quote.

Squirrel removal · Toronto & the GTA

Squirrels in the attic

the 6 a.m. alarm clock you never set

It starts as a few scratches. Then it's running. Then one morning you realize you can follow something's entire commute across your ceiling. Squirrels are daytime animals, so if your attic comes alive at sunrise and settles at dusk, this is almost certainly your guest — and the good news is they're one of the most straightforward removals there is, done kindly.

Call 437-484-9012

How you'll know it's squirrels

You don't need to climb up and confirm it — these signs, noticed from your bed and your driveway, are plenty.

  • Scratching, scampering, or a rolling sound (that's a nut being moved) — mostly early morning and late afternoon
  • Quiet all night, every night: squirrels sleep when you do
  • A chewed roof vent, soffit, or fascia, or a small hole right at the roof edge
  • The same squirrel running the same roofline, or dropping onto the roof from the same tree branch
  • Leaves and shredded insulation gathered into a nest, if anyone's peeked into the attic
  • Chewed wiring or wood up there — squirrels chew constantly, and this is the sign that makes it urgent

Getting them out, kindly

No traps, no poison, no drama. Four steps, and the squirrels do most of the work themselves.

1

A proper look, first

The pro inspects the attic and roofline to confirm it's squirrels, find every way in — there's usually more than one — and check for pups. Baby squirrels can't leave on their own, and finding them now changes the plan for the better.

2

The one-way door

A small door goes over the main entry: out is easy, back in is impossible. The squirrels leave to feed, as they do every day — and that evening, home is closed. Every other entry gets sealed with chew-proof screening at the same visit.

3

If there are babies

Pups are placed safely outside, right by the entry, in a warm box. Their mother finds them — she is listening for them — and carries them one by one to a backup nest, usually within hours. Nobody is separated for good.

4

Sealed, and quiet again

Once the attic is confirmed clear, the door comes off and the entry is sealed for good. If nesting shredded your insulation, cleanup or replacement can be quoted then — only if it's actually needed.

Squirrel questions, answered straight

Why not just trap and release them?

Because Ontario law says a captured animal must be released within 1 km of capture, within 24 hours — and a squirrel released a few streets away treats it as a short commute. It's home by dinner. The one-way door plus sealed entries is what actually ends it.

It's spring and I think there are babies. What happens?

That's the most common situation of all, and the process is built for it: mum leaves through the one-way door, the pups wait safely in a reunion box by the entry, and she relocates them herself. The final seal-up simply waits until the attic is confirmed empty. Mention babies in the form — there's a field for exactly that.

Will they just chew a brand-new hole?

They'll try the old spots first — which is why every entry, not just the main one, gets sealed in chew-proof material. Trimming branches that bridge to your roof removes their favourite highway, and your pro will point out which ones matter.

How fast do I need to act?

This week rather than this month. Squirrels' teeth never stop growing, so neither does the chewing — and wiring damage is a genuine fire risk. If you're hearing activity daily, pick “hearing activity daily” in the form and mean it.

Raccoon removal · Toronto & the GTA

Raccoons in the attic

sounds like a person up there, doesn't it?

That's the giveaway. Raccoons are big, strong, and nocturnal — heavy thumps and slow walking overhead at night, torn shingles by day. Toronto has one of the densest raccoon populations anywhere, and to a raccoon your warm attic reads exactly like a hollow tree. Here's the thing to hold onto: this is fixable, it's routine work for a GTA pro, and it does not require you to meet the tenant in person. Please don't.

Call 437-484-9012

How you'll know it's raccoons

Raccoons don't do subtle. If several of these sound familiar, you can be fairly confident before anyone inspects.

  • Heavy thumping, walking, or dragging sounds at night — far louder than mice or squirrels
  • Torn shingles, ripped soffits, bent roof vents, or a lifted chimney cap
  • A strong, sour odour — raccoons use one corner of the attic as a latrine
  • Raccoons seen climbing to the roof at dusk, or tipped green bins on collection night
  • In spring: chattering and soft crying — a mother with kits, and the attic goes quiet only when they're asleep
  • Insulation torn up and tunnelled through, visible from the attic hatch

Getting them out, kindly

Raccoon work is squirrel work's stronger, more careful sibling — same humane idea, heavier materials, and one non-negotiable rule: the family leaves together.

1

A careful inspection

The pro locates the den, maps the entry damage, and — from roughly March through July — checks for kits. A mother raccoon will not abandon her young, so any plan that ignores them fails; the plan starts with them.

2

The door, and the reunion box

A reinforced one-way door lets the mother out to feed. The kits are gathered gently and placed in a heated reunion box right outside the entry — she collects them herself and carries them to a backup den, usually that same night.

3

Sealed against strong hands

Raccoons can rip open what stops a squirrel, so vents, soffits, and the chimney get heavy-gauge screening and proper caps. Every entry is closed, not just the one she was using.

4

Cleanup, handled safely

Raccoon droppings can carry roundworm eggs, so attic cleanup is specialist work with proper equipment — not a weekend job with a dust mask. If the den was established, your pro can quote decontamination and insulation replacement.

Raccoon questions, answered straight

Should I go up and have a look myself?

No — honestly, this is the one firm “don't” on this page. A cornered mother is protective and strong, and the latrine corner carries roundworm risk. Everything a pro needs to know first, you can describe from downstairs: when it's loud, where it sounds heaviest, what the roof looks like from the ground. The form asks for exactly that.

What actually happens to the babies?

They stay with their mother — that's the whole design. Kits wait in a warm reunion box by the entry; mum, who knows their voices, moves them one at a time to a den she already has elsewhere. Sealing only happens once the attic is confirmed empty and quiet.

Why my house, though?

Nothing personal, and nothing you did wrong. Toronto's raccoon density is famously high, and a loose soffit, an uncapped chimney, and a tree touching the roof is — to a raccoon — a vacancy sign on a perfect hollow tree. The seal-up step takes down the sign.

Can I wait until the kits grow up and leave?

A litter can stay for months, and the damage, odour, and droppings accumulate the whole time — then autumn denning season starts the cycle again. Handled in baby season, with the reunion method, they leave this week instead. Sooner is both kinder and cheaper.

Skunk removal · Toronto & the GTA

Skunks under the deck

you smelled this guest before you saw it

Skunks are the ground-floor tenants. They don't climb into attics — they dig a quiet, dark den under a deck, porch, shed, or set of concrete steps, come out at night to hunt grubs in your lawn, and would honestly rather be left alone. The smell is the headline, but a spray is a skunk's last resort, not its hobby. Handled calmly — family kept together, den screened so it stays empty — this is routine, humane work, and nobody has to get sprayed doing it. Least of all your dog.

Call 437-484-9012

How you'll know it's a skunk

With skunks, your nose usually knows first. These signs, noticed around the yard and the deck, are plenty — no need to go peering under anything.

  • A strong, musky skunk smell hanging around the deck, porch, or yard — strongest at night and early morning, even when nothing has actually sprayed
  • A dug opening under a deck, porch, shed, or concrete steps, with loose soil fanned out beside it
  • Small cone-shaped holes dug in the lawn overnight — a skunk hunting grubs and insects just under the surface
  • A slow, waddling black-and-white shape crossing the yard at dusk, unbothered and in no hurry at all
  • Your dog suddenly obsessed with one gap in the deck or fence line, especially after dark
  • In late spring and early summer: a line of small kits trailing their mother across the yard at dusk

Getting them out, kindly

Same humane idea as the attic animals, adapted to a ground den: the skunks leave on their own at night, the family stays together, and the den is screened so the next skunk doesn't move into the vacancy.

1

A careful look, first

The pro confirms it's a skunk den, finds every opening in and out, and checks for kits. Skunk kits are born in late spring and can't follow their mother out for their first weeks — finding them now decides the timing, so nobody gets sealed in and nobody gets separated.

2

Every opening but one, closed

All the den's entrances are screened shut except the main one. That way there's exactly one way out — through the door in the next step — and no side door back in.

3

The one-way door on the den

A one-way door goes over the main opening: out is easy, back in is impossible. The skunk heads out at dusk to feed, as it does every night, and comes home to a closed door. If there are kits old enough to follow, they trail out behind her; if they're still too young, the door simply waits until they are — the family leaves together, or the job waits.

4

Screened against digging

Once the den is confirmed empty, the door comes off and the real fix goes in: heavy-gauge screening trenched down and out around the deck, porch, or shed — an underground barrier a skunk can't dig past. An open, unscreened den is a vacancy sign to the next skunk; screening is what makes this a one-time fix. Securing bins and pet food, and dealing with a grub-heavy lawn, removes the other invitations.

Until the visit: don't get sprayed

A skunk sprays when it's cornered or rushed — almost every spray story involves a dog charging in. A calm yard is a smell-free yard.

Do this

  • Give it a wide berth. Skunks are slow, short-sighted, and genuinely not looking for trouble. If you see one, just back away and let it waddle off.
  • Check the yard before letting the dog out at night. Light on, quick look, then out. Keep dogs leashed after dark while a den is active.
  • Watch for the warning signs. Foot-stamping, hissing, and a raised tail mean "back off" — a skunk would rather warn you than spray.
  • Take away the buffet. Secure green bins, bring pet food in, and clear fallen fruit — an easy food source is half the reason a yard gets chosen.

Please don't

  • Don't corner, chase, or try to shoo it off. That's exactly what turns a calm skunk into a spray — usually right where you live.
  • Don't block the den opening yourself. You could trap kits — or a very annoyed adult — under your own deck, and the smell problem gets far worse.
  • Don't set your own trap. A trapped skunk is a stressed skunk, Ontario law requires release within 1 km within 24 hours anyway, and an unscreened den just gets a new tenant.
  • Don't use mothballs, ammonia rags, or poison. They don't evict skunks, they're a hazard to pets and kids, and they make the den area smell worse, not better.

Skunk questions, answered straight

Will it spray my dog or my kids?

Almost certainly not, if nobody rushes it. Spraying is a last resort — a skunk only carries so much, and it would rather stamp its feet, hiss, and waddle away. Nearly every spray incident is a dog charging straight in. Keep dogs leashed or checked at night while the den is active, and the risk stays very low.

It's spring and I think there are kits under there. What happens?

That's the most common skunk situation of all, and the timing is built around it. If the kits are still too young to follow their mother out, the one-way door waits until they can — then the whole family leaves together at dusk. Nothing is sealed while anything is still inside. Mention kits in the form — there's a field for exactly that.

Something already got sprayed. What do I do about the smell?

Air the area out first — most outdoor spray smell fades over days to a couple of weeks. For a sprayed dog, use a pet-safe de-skunking wash (tomato juice mostly just masks it). If the spray happened right at the den under your deck, odour cleanup under the structure can be quoted after inspection, along with the removal.

Why not just trap it and let it go somewhere else?

Because Ontario law says a captured animal must be released within 1 km of capture, within 24 hours — close enough that it can simply come back. And even if it didn't, the open den under your deck would be taken by the next skunk within the season. The one-way door plus digging-proof screening is what actually ends it.
